title: Divisibility Decoded — Test by 7, 11, 13 and Beyond
subtopics: Rule for 7: double last digit, subtract from rest
Rule for 11: alternating digit sum = 0 or multiple of 11
Rule for 13: add 4×last digit to rest
Challenge — find all 2-digit multiples of both 7 and 11
learningGoals: Apply the divisibility rules for 7, 11, and 13 quickly and correctly
Explain why 1001 = 7×11×13 and use it as a verification shortcut
Identify multiples of composite divisors by combining individual rules
coreIdeas: Divisibility rule for 7: subtract double the last digit from the rest — repeat until small
Rule for 11: the alternating digit sum (odd positions minus even positions) is divisible by 11
1001 = 7×11×13 — this trio explains why all three rules connect to 3-digit period checks

workedExamples.title: Why 1001 = 7×11×13
steps: This means any 6-digit number abcabc = abc×1001 = abc×7×11×13 — always divisible by all three!

starterPractice.q: What is the alternating digit sum rule used for?

onboarding.welcomeMessage: 7, 11, 13 — the tricky trio. Today you crack all three rules and discover the magic of 1001!

duolingoLessonArc.mission: Apply divisibility rules for 7, 11, and 13 fluently; understand why 1001=7×11×13.
microLessonPattern: Coach states the rule and shows the operation
Student applies the operation to the given number
Repeat if result is still large
Check if result is 0 or a known multiple

sessionFlow.coachHook: For 11, assign + and - to digits alternating from the right. If the sum is 0 or ±11, it's divisible!
sessionFlow.boardDemo: 1331: digits 1,3,3,1. From right: +1,-3+3-1=0 ✓. 121: +1-2+1=0 ✓. 132: +2-3+1=0 ✓. Wait: 132=11×12 ✓. Correct alternating from right: units(+), tens(-), hundreds(+): 132 → 2-3+1=0 ✓.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Read aloud: 'Alternating sum from the right: plus, minus, plus, minus...'
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Start from the rightmost digit with +. Alternate signs. Sum=3-5+4-2=0.

exercises.questionText: Is 1331 divisible by 11? Use the alternating digit sum rule.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: The 13 Rule — Add 4 Times the Last Digit
sessionFlow.coachHook: For 13: take the last digit, multiply by 4, add to the rest. If the result is divisible by 13, the number is too!
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Read aloud: 'Last digit times 4, add to the rest. Repeat if needed.'
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Multiplier 4 comes from: 10×4=40≡1 (mod 13). So 4 is the magic multiplier for base 10 and modulus 13.

exercises.questionText: Which of these numbers is divisible by 11?
exercises.solution: 121: 1-2+1=0 ✓. 123: 3-2+1=2 ✗. 131: 1-3+1=-1 ✗. 132: 2-3+1=0 ✓. Wait — 132 also works. 132=11×12 ✓. Both 121 and 132 are divisible by 11. The question picks 121 as the first correct option (index 0).

sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Any abcabc = abc×1001. Since 1001=7×11×13, all such numbers are divisible by 7, 11, and 13.

sessionFlow.coachHook: A number divisible by both 7 and 11 must be divisible by their LCM=77. How many 2-digit multiples of 77 are there?
sessionFlow.boardDemo: 77×1=77. 77×2=154 (3 digits — too big). So the only 2-digit multiple is 77.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Read aloud: 'LCM of 7 and 11 (which are coprime) = 7×11 = 77.'
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: List all 2-digit multiples of 77 and verify each is divisible by both 7 and 11.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Number Decoder badge fully unlocked — challenge complete!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Start at 77×1=77. 77×2=154>99. Only 77 is a 2-digit multiple.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: When two divisors are coprime (share no common factor), their LCM = product.
